items.title: Can an Agent Debug a Web Corpus? Agentic Auditing of Slovak FineWeb2
items.summary: Multilingual pipelines such as FineWeb2 apply one recipe across a thousand languages, leaving the failure modes of individual languages unanticipated. We use an LLM once, as a corpus debugger rather than a classifier: a tool-using agent explores the corpus through a read-only, budgeted API and compiles each finding into an executable test, which a native speaker then validates. On the 26.5M-document Slovak portion of FineWeb2, three runs costing \$2.21-\$2.84 each found seven findings over four phenomena. The largest is a machine-generated content farm of 1,408,437 documents (5.32%) that passed the pipeline's filters, 86.6% of it passing even stricter thresholds. Blinded labels support 6 of the 7 findings (defect rates .53-1.00 against .08 in a random control) and do not support one. The compiled suite scans the full corpus in 0.7 s of wall-clock time without a GPU, against \$12k-\$90k per LLM classification pass. The best static sampling baseline validates more selectors than any agent run, at under half the cost. The agent contributes exact prevalence, a precision estimate checked against sampled documents, an account of why the pipeline missed each slice, and a reusable test. We release the framework, Slovak test suite, validation data and agent trajectories.

items.title: Bridging Foundational and Agentic Capabilities of LLMs
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents, yet it remains unclear how their foundational capabilities translate into agentic capabilities. End-to-end scores leave unresolved whether low benchmark capability or weak deployment drives a failure, limiting actionable diagnosis. We bridge foundational and agentic capabilities through an operation-level measurement framework. We represent each model with a foundational profile derived from capability benchmarks and an operation profile derived from interaction trajectories, and define capability realization gaps as deviations of observed operation performance from predictions based on foundational capabilities. Experiments on fifteen model services in $τ^2$-Bench show that foundational profiles only partially predict agentic operations. Models with comparable profiles can differ substantially in execution, and these gaps remain consistent across task subsets. Operation profiles add information and substantially improve task-score prediction. The framework locates execution departures at the operation level to inform model development and agent evaluation. We will release our code and analysis artifacts.

items.title: Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement
items.summary: LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype. Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination. Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.

Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. items.title: Day-0 Support for Flint on vLLM
items.summary: vLLM supports both Flint checkpoints (40B total, 2.5B active) from day 0, decoding a single request at about 500 tokens/s on one GPU.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:day 0 support for flint on vllm
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Recursive's Flint from day 0 . Both its NVFP4 and BF16 checkpoints run on a single GPU, and a single request decodes at about 500 tokens/s on one GB200, even with 100K tokens of context. Flint is a 40B-parameter MoE that activates only about 2.5B parameters per token, with sliding-window attention in most layers and a 262K-token context. It ships as two separate checkpoints: NVFP4 (quantization-aware trained) and BF16. The day-0 Docker image vllm/vllm-openai:flint (x86_64 and arm64, CUDA 13.0) has Flint support built in: Flint support is being merged into vLLM ( #62938 ). With a vLLM build that includes it, serve the same way: Flint is a 49-layer pre-norm MoE with hidden size 2048. What sets it apart is how little of it looks at the whole context. Figure 1: Flint's layer stack and its two sublayers. Gold marks what differs from a standard pre-norm MoE. Open it full-screen . The NVFP4 checkpoint is a GGUF file whose blocks are NVIDIA's NVFP4 format in a different byte order. vLLM repacks it losslessly at load time and runs it weight-only (W4A16), with BF16 activations and KV cache, as Recursive's reference implementation does. Every Flint kernel follows the reference's rounding points, and accuracy matches it on GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond, long-context MRCR and a tool-calling suite. Our first implementation, built from vLLM's stock layers, was slow at small batch sizes: a decode step ran 1,096 kernels, many of them tuned for much larger batches. We replaced them with Flint-specific kernels one change at a time, checking each against the reference. Figure 2: Model-forward latency on one GB200 after each change, for batch-1 decode at 100K context and an 8,192-token prefill. Toggle the checkpoint, or show the table for every shape. Open it full-screen . For up to 8 requests, the low-latency path runs each MoE layer as seven kernels: Q/K norm, RoPE, routing and the expert combine are fused into the neighboring GEMV kernels. Each kernel is launched with programmatic dependent launch, so it loads its weights while the previous one is still running. In total, NVFP4 decode went from 4.81 to 1.78 ms (2.7×), BF16 decode from 3.53 to 2.34 ms (1.5×), and an 8K-token prefill from 207 to 145 ms (1.4×). A forward now runs 346 kernels instead of 1,096. Served end to end, batch-1 decode at 100K context takes 2.06 ms per token (about 485 tokens/s), which is the forward plus the LM head and sampling. items.title: How Numan Built an Eval-First AI Health Coach with LangGraph and LangSmith
items.summary: How Numan built Nu, an AI health coach, on LangGraph and LangSmith with per-category evals, simulated conversations, and safety gates on a regulatory line.
items.story_key: model:langgraph|title:how numan built an eval first ai health coach with langgraph and langsmith
items.content_excerpt: Numan is a UK digital health company helping patients manage long-term conditions across weight, hormones, and sexual health. Many of our patients are on a weight-loss programme and use the app daily to track progress. When building Nu, our AI health coach, one of our design challenges was delivering high-quality health coaching without crossing the line into medical diagnosis, prescriptions, or making clinical decisions—all strict boundaries for agents in our highly regulated medical space. While we initially focused on the agent and automation around it, what turned out to matter most was the quality of our evaluation criteria. This is the story of how we developed and improved our evaluation criteria to deliver high-quality user experiences while steering clear of areas subject to regulation. We started where most teams start, with a dataset of inputs and expected outputs, and an LLM judge scoring each reply. While that playbook works well for a Q&A agent, coaching is a conversation, not an answer. Every approach that fixed Nu's reply in advance failed in two ways: 1. Single-turn evals on static fixtures (a fixed input, a fixed expected output, and a judge scoring one reply on its own). Behavioural coaching rarely has one right answer to a prompt and whether a reply was safe depends on the conversation around it. Nu needs to understand what is getting in the patient’s way across a conversation before it advises and hold the right boundary when a patient pushes. Averaging one score across the whole dataset hid where Nu failed. A few bad replies barely move the number, so the conversation looks compliant when it isn’t. The fixtures also caused a second problem. In one run, a cluster of low scores turned out to be the eval’s fault, not Nu’s. The rubric expected empathy, exploration and advice all within a two-turn exchange, whereas a human coach would pace these across a conversation. Nu was coaching properly, but the narrow, fixed eval signaled failures incorrectly. 2. Scripted multi-turn conversations. The obvious fix for single-turn fixtures is to write out a patient’s expected series of replies in advance. With this "script," several turns of a scenario, fed to Nu one at a time, allow the judge to score the full transcript at the end. While this gives the judge more room than a single reply, the eval fell apart the same way. items.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
items.summary: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

items.title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
items.summary:
In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation.
  We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92).
  We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

items.title: vllm v0.32.0
items.summary:
v0.32.0

Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

  • Structured decisions and generic parsers: the new POST /v1/systemone endpoint answers choice, noul and score questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on Cloudflare/clef-omni (#61064), LiquidAI/d1-3B (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new hf tool and reasoning parser (--tool-call-parser hf, --reasoning-parser hf) reads the checkpoint's response_template, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
  • Low-precision KV cache everywhere: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); fp8_ds_mla on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit ultraquant_4bit KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#57057).
  • Model Runner V2: a GPU n-gram speculator with variable-length drafts (#40704), Elastic EP (#53934), pipeline parallelism with prefill context parallelism for MLA models (#59139), a stock torch.compile mode (#59079), and MRV2 is now the default on ROCm with the model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360).
  • Faster startup and serving: vllm download-kernels installs FlashInfer's precompiled kernels (#58765); vllm preload --preload-autotune keeps the FlashInfer autotune table warm across restarts (#60085); a shared-memory tensor arena broadcasts large multimodal tensors to workers with one copy (#51207); tokenizers and processors load from the local snapshot (#60825); and with --api-server-count above 1 each connection goes to the least-loaded API worker, for 43-85% more req/s on short requests (Qwen3-0.6B, 32 input / 1 output tokens) in the PR's benchmark (#60723).
  • Model support: new EmbeddingGemma 2 omni-modal embeddings (#60254), MiniCPM-V 4.7 (#58674) and Nemotron 3.5 ASR (#59827); video input in the Transformers modeling backend (#57441); GLM-5.3 sparse MLA index conversions reused across layers (3.5-3.9x on that kernel, #59464) and fused multi-step draft decode (13.3% at concurrency 1, #57443); HiSparse per-request residency caching for up to 58% more throughput on GLM-5.3-NVFP4 on B200 with long, fully GPU-resident contexts at high concurrency (#60083).
